'''Hartley Rogers Jr.''' (July 6, 1926 – July 17, 2015) was an American mathematician who worked in [[computability theory]], and was a professor in the [[MIT Mathematics Department|Mathematics Department]] of the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]].

==Early life and education ==
Born in 1926 in [[Buffalo, New York]], Rogers studied English as an undergraduate at [[Yale University]], graduating in 1946. After visiting the [[University of Cambridge]] under a [[Henry Fellowship]], he returned to Yale for a master's degree in physics, which he completed in 1950. He studied mathematics under [[Alonzo Church]] at [[Princeton University|Princeton]], earned a second master's degree in 1951,<ref name=math-faculty/> and received his Ph.D. there in 1952.<ref name=mg>{{MathGenealogy|id=8021}}</ref>

== Career ==
He was a Benjamin Peirce Lecturer at [[Harvard University]] from 1952 to 1955. After holding a visiting position at MIT, he became a professor in the [[MIT Mathematics Department]] in 1956.<ref name=math-faculty/> His doctoral students included [[Patrick C. Fischer|Patrick Fischer]], [[Louis Hodes]], [[Carl Jockusch]], [[Andrew Kahr]], [[David Luckham]], [[Rohit Jivanlal Parikh|Rohit Parikh]], [[David Park (computer scientist)|David Park]], and [[John Stillwell]].<ref name=mg/> He chaired the MIT faculty senate from 1971 to 1973 and served as associate provost of the university from 1974 to 1980.<ref name=math-faculty/>

== Personal life ==
Beyond teaching and research, Rogers was an avid rower and rowing competitor.<ref name=math-faculty/>

He retired as a [[professor emeritus]] in 2009, and died on July 17, 2015.<ref name=math-faculty>{{cite web|url=https://math.mit.edu/about/history/obituaries/rogers.php|title=Hartley Rogers, Jr., Professor Emeritus of Mathematics|date=July 22, 2015|publisher=MIT Mathematics Department|access-date=2024-06-28}}</ref>

==Mathematical work==
Rogers worked in [[mathematical logic]], particularly [[recursion theory]], and wrote the classic text ''Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability''.<ref>{{cite book |author=Hartley Rogers, Jr. |date=1967 |title=Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability |publisher=McGraw Hill}}</ref> The [[Roger's equivalence theorem|Rogers equivalence theorem]] is named after him.

Rogers won the [[Lester R. Ford Award]] in 1965 for his expository article ''Information Theory''.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Rogers Jr., Hartley|title=Information Theory|journal=[[Mathematics Magazine]]|volume=37|year=1964|issue=2|pages=63–78|doi=10.1080/0025570X.1964.11975485|url=http://www.maa.org/programs/maa-awards/writing-awards/information-theory|url-access=subscription}}</ref>
